title: 1 Samuel 15:1–9
context: Samuel brings Saul a command from the LORD of Armies: strike Amalek and devote everything to destruction, because of what Amalek did to Israel on the way out of Egypt (Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). Saul musters the army, warns the Kenites to leave, and defeats the Amalekites. But he and the people spare King Agag and the best of the livestock, destroying only what was worthless. The section states the herem command plainly; readers in both traditions treat it as a unique judgment tied to Amalek, not a model for today.

verses.text: Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you to be king over his people, over Israel. Now therefore listen to the voice of the LORD’s words.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel reminds Saul that the LORD sent him to anoint Saul as king, so Saul must listen to the LORD’s words. Arminian readers note that the reminder frames the coming command as a test of whether Saul will freely obey the God who appointed him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s authority as derived from God’s appointment, placing Saul under the LORD’s word rather than above it. Shared ground: the opening sets up the chapter’s main theme, obedience to the voice of the LORD.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says, ‘I remember what Amalek did to Israel, how he set himself against him on the way when he came up out of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD remembers what Amalek did when Israel came out of Egypt. Arminian readers note that this recalls the attack in Exodus 17:8–16 and the command to remember it in Deuteronomy 25:17–19, long before Saul’s time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s memory as his faithfulness to his word about Amalek, carried out in his chosen time. Both traditions read the verse as grounding the command in a specific history between Israel and Amalek, not in general hostility.

verses.text: Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The command is to destroy Amalek completely, including women, children, and livestock. Arminian readers state the text plainly and acknowledge its moral weight; many also note that Amalek appears again later (27:8; 30:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm God’s right to judge and read the command as tied to Amalek’s history alone. Shared ground: both traditions treat this herem command as a unique judgment in redemptive history and never as a model for violence by anyone today.

verses.text: Saul summoned the people, and counted them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul musters the army at Telaim, whose location is uncertain, though it seems to lie in the south. Arminian readers note that he responds quickly to the command, at least in gathering the troops, with a large force.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the separate count of men from Judah. Both traditions acknowledge that the large numbers in Samuel are read in different ways by careful interpreters, and neither stakes theological claims on the exact figures given here.

verses.text: Saul came to the city of Amalek, and set an ambush in the valley.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul comes to the city of Amalek and sets an ambush in the valley. Arminian readers note the practical military steps Saul takes, showing that the problem in this chapter is not his willingness to fight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the campaign beginning in a way that seems obedient, so the later failure is all the more striking. Shared ground: the city of Amalek is not named, and the narrative focuses on Saul’s conduct rather than on geography.

verses.text: Saul said to the Kenites, “Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them; for you showed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt.” So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul warns the Kenites to leave because they showed kindness to Israel in the wilderness. Arminian readers see justice that distinguishes between peoples, recalling the Kenite connection to Moses’ family (Judges 1:16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s judgment on Amalek does not sweep up those who had shown kindness to his people. Both traditions read Saul’s warning as a right act, showing that the command was aimed at a specific people, not at everyone nearby.

verses.text: Saul struck the Amalekites, from Havilah as you go to Shur, which is before Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul strikes the Amalekites from Havilah toward Shur, near Egypt. Arminian readers note that the same phrase describes Ishmael’s territory in Genesis 25:18, though the exact limits of these regions remain uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a wide victory granted by God. Shared ground: the geographic summary marks a broad campaign, while later chapters show that some Amalekites remained, so many read the language as describing the sweep of the battle.

verses.text: He took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul takes Agag alive and destroys the people with the sword. Arminian readers note the tension already visible: the people are struck down, yet their king is spared, against the plain terms of the command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul’s partial obedience emerging, as he keeps the king who embodied Amalek’s hostility. Both traditions read the verse as stating the violence soberly while pointing to the problem of selective obedience that follows.

verses.text: But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep, of the cattle, of the fat calves, of the lambs, and all that was good, and were not willing to utterly destroy them; but everything that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul and the people spare Agag and the best livestock, destroying only what is worthless. Arminian readers stress that this is a deliberate choice: they were “not willing” to obey fully, preferring what seemed valuable to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart of the sin in substituting human judgment for God’s command. Shared ground: the verse defines Saul’s failure as keeping what God had devoted to him, and both traditions treat that failure as real disobedience.
